summary: Names the data types used in RADIUS attributes, which implementations had long used without formal definitions. It updates earlier RADIUS specifications to match practice, building on the types in RFC 6158.

plainLanguage.summary: Every value in a RADIUS message has a type, such as a number, a piece of text or an address. Each specification named those types in its own way, and nobody kept the list. This document writes the list down once, and gives IANA a place to keep it.

questions: what data types does radius define
what is the radius tlv format
subtitle: A shared, IANA-managed list of the data types that RADIUS attributes carry, written down after two decades of unwritten practice.

tldr.problem: RADIUS attributes had always carried typed data such as integers, text and addresses, but the types were named inconsistently across specifications and were not managed anywhere.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8044 names and defines 17 data types, creates an IANA Data Type registry for them, and adds a Data Type column to the RADIUS Attribute Types registry.
tldr.outcome: New RADIUS specifications MUST define attributes using these types. The document mandates no changes to existing implementations, since it records existing practice.

today: RFC 8044 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 2865, RFC 3162, RFC 4072, RFC 6158, RFC 6572 and RFC 7268, and it permits the types in the new registry to count as the basic data types described in RFC 6158.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RADIUS specifications have historically defined attributes in terms of name, value and data type. Of those three pieces of information, the name is recorded by IANA in the 'RADIUS Attribute Types' registry but is not otherwise managed or restricted. The value is managed by IANA and recorded in that registry. The data type is not managed or recorded in the 'RADIUS Attribute Types' registry. Experience has shown that there is a need to create well-known data types and have them managed by IANA.

The document defines an IANA RADIUS 'Data Type' registry and updates the 'RADIUS Attribute Types' registry to use those newly defined data types. It recommends how both specifications and implementations should use the data types, and it extends the 'RADIUS Attribute Types' registry to have a data type for each assigned attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS attributes have a name, a value and a type. IANA kept the name and the value but not the type, so this document adds a place for the type and fills it in.

sections.title: Specification and Implementation Problems
sections.content:
When attributes are defined in specifications, the terms 'Value' and 'String' are used to refer to the contents of an attribute. However, these names are used recursively and inconsistently, so defining a field to recursively contain itself is problematic. A number of data type names and definitions are given in the original RADIUS specification, which are named and clearly defined, but that practice was not continued in later specifications. That specification defines attributes of data type 'address' to carry IPv4 addresses, yet the RADIUS and IPv6 specification defines attributes of data type 'Address' to carry IPv6 addresses. The use of the word 'address' for disparate data types is problematic.

Other failures are that the RADIUS and IPv6 specification gives no data type name and definition for the data types IPv6 address, Interface-Id or IPv6 prefix; the RADIUS Extensions specification defines Event-Timestamp to carry a time but does not reuse the 'time' data type, instead repeating the definition; and the RADIUS Support for Proxy Mobile IPv6 specification defines multiple attributes that carry IPv4 prefixes without naming or defining an 'IPv4 prefix' data type. These ambiguities and inconsistencies need to be resolved.

RADIUS implementations often use dictionaries to map attribute names to type values and define data types for each attribute. The data types in those dictionaries are defined by each implementation but correspond to the ad hoc data types used in the specifications. In effect, implementations have seen the need for well-defined data types and have created them. It is time for RADIUS specifications to follow this practice.

The document mandates no changes to any past, present or future RADIUS implementation. It instead documents existing practice in order to simplify the process of writing RADIUS specifications, clarify the interpretation of RADIUS standards, and improve the communication between specification authors and IANA. Implementations SHOULD use the data types defined here, in preference to any ad hoc data types currently in use, which should have a minimal effect since most ad hoc data types are compatible with the ones defined here. Any difference will typically be limited to the name of the data type.
sections.plainLanguage: Two specifications both called their type 'address' but meant different things, and other specifications never gave a name for their types at all. Software makers had already worked out their own list, so the document writes that list down in the open.

sections.title: Use of Data Types in Specifications
sections.content:
Previous specifications used inconsistent and conflicting names for the contents of RADIUS attributes. The term 'Value' was used to define a field that carries the contents of an attribute, and then used in later sections as the subfield of attribute contents, so the field ended up defined as recursively containing itself. Similarly, 'String' was used both as a data type and as a subfield of other data types.

The document corrects this by using context-specific names for the fields of attributes and data types, so that, for example, a field called 'VSA-Data' must contain different data from a field called 'EVS-Data'. It defines the term Attr-Data as the Value field of an Attribute as defined in the original RADIUS specification, whose contents MUST be of a valid data type as defined in the RADIUS 'Data Type' registry, and uses it consistently in place of the more ambiguous name 'Value'. 'Value' is used consistently to refer to the contents of a simple data type, such as an 'integer', while for data types that carry complex information the fields are named after the data type.

New RADIUS specifications MUST define attributes using data types from the RADIUS 'Data Type' registry. A specification may define a new data type, update the registry and use the new type, all in the same document. Attributes can usually be completely described by the Attribute Type value, name and data type, so the use of ASCII art is then limited to the definition of new data types and for complex data types. Because an attribute can be allocated from any of the extended spaces with more than one option for the attribute header format, and the allocation decision is made after the specification has been accepted for publication, it is essentially impossible to create the correct ASCII art before final publication. It is therefore RECOMMENDED that ASCII art diagrams not be used for new RADIUS attribute specifications.

When defining a new attribute, the fields Description, Type, Length, Data Type and Value SHOULD be given. The Description field gives the meaning and interpretation of the attribute. The Type field is the Attribute Type value in the dotted number notation, which specifications can often leave as 'TBD'. The Length field describes the length of the attribute, with a maximum length SHOULD be given for attributes of variable length. The Data Type field is one of the named data types from the registry. The Value field describes any attribute-specific limitations on the values carried by the data type, and where the values are limited to a subset of the possible range, valid ranges MUST be defined. For attributes of data type 'enum', a list of enumerated values and names MUST be given.

When a specification needs to define a new data type it SHOULD follow the format used in the document, giving the Name, Value, Length and Format fields along with values, and describing the expected use and why a new data type is required. The Name field SHOULD be a single name, all lowercase, and contractions such as 'ipv4addr' are RECOMMENDED where they add clarity. A new data type should be defined only when absolutely necessary, and it is RECOMMENDED that vendors do not define vendor-specific data types, because those are rarely necessary and can cause interoperability problems. Any new data type MUST have a unique name in the registry, and IANA assigns the number.
sections.plainLanguage: New specifications must name the type of every attribute from the shared list, and they must stop drawing the attributes as pictures of boxes, because the final numbers are not known until the document is published.

sections.title: Use of Data Types in Implementations
sections.content:
Implementations that do not support a particular data type MUST treat attributes of that data type as being of data type 'string'. It is RECOMMENDED that such attributes be treated as invalid attributes.

Where the contents of a data type do not match the definition, implementations MUST treat the enclosing attribute as being an invalid attribute. This requirement includes, but is not limited to, attributes with values outside the allowed ranges for the data type, as given in the data types 'integer', 'ipv4addr', 'ipv6addr', 'ipv4prefix', 'ipv6prefix' or 'enum'; 'text' attributes where the contents do not match the required format; and attributes where the length is shorter or longer than the allowed lengths for the given data type.

The requirements for Reserved fields are more difficult to quantify. Implementations SHOULD be able to receive and process attributes where Reserved fields are non-zero, but no 'correct' processing of such attributes is defined. Instead, specifications that define one or more new meanings for Reserved fields SHOULD describe how each new meaning is compatible with older implementations. Implementations MUST set Reserved fields to zero when creating attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver that does not recognise a type treats the value as opaque bytes. A value that does not fit the definition of its type makes the whole attribute invalid, and the receiver drops it.

sections.title: Data Type Definitions
sections.content:
The document defines 17 data types, each with a definition, a name, a number, a length and an encoding format. These definitions have no impact on existing RADIUS implementations, and there is no requirement that implementations use these names. Where possible the name of each data type has been taken from previous specifications; in some cases a different name has been chosen, sometimes to avoid ambiguity such as 'address' versus 'Address', otherwise for compatibility with the original RADIUS specification or with common implementation usage.

The numbers assigned to the data types have no meaning other than to let IANA track them, because RADIUS does not encode information about data types in a packet, so the numbers will never occur in a packet. The encoding of each data type is taken from previous specifications, and the fields are transmitted from left to right. Where the data types have interdependencies, the simplest data type is given first and dependent ones later.

The simplest types are 'integer', 'enum', 'time', 'text' and 'string'. The 'integer' type encodes a 32-bit unsigned integer in network byte order, and 'enum' encodes the same thing but is used for enumerated types such as Service-Type. The 'time' type encodes time as a 32-bit unsigned value in seconds since 00:00:00 UTC on January 1, 1970; because it is unsigned it is not subject to the signed integer overflow in the year 2038. The 'text' type encodes UTF-8 text and is limited to no more than 253 octets when the attribute is allocated in the standard space. The 'string' type encodes binary data as a sequence of undistinguished octets and carries the same 253-octet limit in the standard space.

Neither 'text' nor 'string' terminates with a NUL octet, because the attribute has a Length field and does not use a terminator, and text or strings of length zero MUST NOT be sent: the entire attribute should be omitted instead. Where there is a need to encapsulate complex data structures and TLVs cannot be used, the 'string' data type MUST be used.

The 'concat' type permits the transport of more than 253 octets of data in a standard space attribute, and is otherwise identical to 'string'. If multiple attributes of this type are contained in a packet, all attributes of the same type code MUST be in order and MUST be consecutive. As a rough guide it is RECOMMENDED that this data type transport no more than 2048 octets of data. It MUST NOT be used for attributes in the short extended or long extended spaces, nor in any field or subfield of the 'tlv', 'vsa', 'extended', 'long-extended' or 'evs' types.

The address and prefix types are 'ifid', 'ipv4addr', 'ipv6addr', 'ipv6prefix' and 'ipv4prefix'. The 'ifid' type encodes an Interface-Id as an 8-octet IPv6 Interface Identifier. The 'ipv6prefix' type is at least two and no more than eighteen octets, with a one-octet Reserved field that is always zero, a one-octet Prefix-Length of at least 0 and no larger than 128, and a Prefix of up to 16 octets. The 'ipv4prefix' type is six octets: a Reserved octet, a Prefix-Length octet, and a fixed 4-octet Prefix, where bits outside the Prefix-Length MUST be zero.

The remaining types are 'integer64', a 64-bit unsigned integer in eight octets, and the structural types 'tlv', 'vsa', 'extended', 'long-extended' and 'evs'. The 'tlv' type is at least three octets, with a one-octet TLV-Type, a one-octet TLV-Length that MUST have a value between 3 and 255, and one or more octets of TLV-Data. The 'vsa' type is at least five octets: a 4-octet Network Management Private Enterprise Code, a one-octet Vendor-Type, and one or more octets of VSA-Data. The 'evs' type is at least six octets and encodes an Extended-Vendor-Specific Attribute, used solely to extend the vendor-specific space. The document does not create data types for the tagged attributes, nor for some attributes with a complex structure such as CHAP-Password, ARAP-Features or Location-Information, because in some cases it is better to treat such complex attributes as being of type 'string'.
sections.plainLanguage: Seventeen named types, from plain numbers and text through to IP addresses, prefixes and structures that wrap other values. Each one says exactly how many bytes it uses and how they are laid out.

sections.title: The Updated Registries
sections.content:
The document defines a new IANA registry located under 'RADIUS Types', called 'Data Type', with registration procedures of Standards Action. The registry contains three columns: Value, the number of the data type, which is an artifact of the registry with no on-the-wire meaning; Description, the name of the data type, which is used only for the registry and has no on-the-wire meaning; and Reference, the specification where the data type was defined. The initial contents are the 17 types described in the document, numbered from 1 for 'integer' through 17 for 'evs'.

The 'RADIUS Attribute Types' registry is updated to have a new column, inserted between the existing 'Description' and 'Reference' columns, named 'Data Type'. The contents of that column are the name of a data type corresponding to the attribute in that row, or blank if the Attribute Type is unassigned. The name of the data type is taken from the 'Data Type' registry. The existing registration requirements for that registry are otherwise unchanged, and IANA now requires that all allocation requests in it contain a Data Type field holding one of the names in the 'Data Type' registry. Updates to the 'Data Type' registry must contain a Value, on which IANA assigns the next unused integer in sequence, a Name, which must be unique in the registry, and a Reference, which is updated with a reference to the document defining the data type.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps two lists: the names of the types, and the type that goes with every numbered attribute.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The specification is concerned solely with updates to IANA registries, so there are no security considerations with the document itself. However, the use of inconsistent names and poorly defined entities in a protocol is problematic, and inconsistencies in specifications can lead to security and interoperability problems in implementations. Further, having one canonical source for the definition of data types means that an implementor has fewer specifications to read, so the implementation work is simpler and more likely to be correct. The goal of the specification is to reduce ambiguities in the RADIUS protocol, which the authors believe will lead to more robust and more secure implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The document itself adds no risk. Its point is that a single clear list makes implementations less likely to disagree about what a value means.

viz.caption: THE RADIUS DATA TYPE REGISTRY (RFC 8044, SECTION 4.1)

items.label: integer
items.desc: A 32-bit unsigned integer in network byte order.

items.label: enum
items.desc: A 32-bit unsigned integer used for enumerated types.

items.label: concat
items.desc: Like string, but permits more than 253 octets.

items.label: ipv6prefix
items.desc: An IPv6 prefix with a length field.

items.label: ipv4prefix
items.desc: An IPv4 prefix with a length field.

viz.caption: THE LENGTHS OF THE FIXED-SIZE TYPES (RFC 8044, SECTION 3)

cells: At least two and no more than eighteen octets

viz.caption: WHAT AN ATTRIBUTE DEFINITION SHOULD CONTAIN (RFC 8044, SECTION 2.1.3)

items.title: Description
items.text: A description of the meaning and interpretation of the attribute.

items.title: Type
items.text: The Attribute Type value in the dotted number notation, often left as TBD for IANA to fill in.

items.title: Length
items.text: A description of the length of the attribute, with a maximum for variable-length attributes.

items.title: Data Type
items.text: One of the named data types from the RADIUS Data Type registry.

items.title: Value
items.text: Any attribute-specific limits on the values. Where the range is limited, the valid ranges must be given.
